title: Taleb Calls H-1B Debate a 'Zero-Sum Fallacy': Foreign Workers Create Jobs
excerpt: The Black Swan author says America's edge rests on other countries' brain drain — and asks whether anti-Indian racism is driving the visa backlash, days after the PERM freeze hit eight major employers.
body:
• Nassim Nicholas Taleb, author of The Black Swan, attacked the US administration's H-1B stance on X, calling it a "zero-sum fallacy" and arguing skilled foreign workers create jobs rather than take them.
  • Taleb said America's technological edge rests on other countries' brain drain, citing Tesla, Einstein, Fermi and von Neumann, and suggested anti-Indian racism may sit behind the visa backlash.
  • His post lands days after the administration suspended PERM green-card processing for Microsoft, Adobe, TCS, Infosys, Wipro, HCLTech, Cognizant and Capgemini.
  • What it means for you: the PERM freeze does not cancel existing H-1B status, but employees of the eight named firms cannot move forward with employer-sponsored green cards while it lasts.

Nassim Nicholas Taleb has entered the H-1B fight. In a post on X on Friday, the author of The Black Swan accused the Trump administration of being "trapped in the ZERO-SUM FALLACY" over skilled-worker visas, arguing that foreign professionals expand the US economy instead of displacing American workers.

"You are NOT taking a job from a citizen, rather creating jobs by increasing overall economic output. Plus, these people (even vegetarians) SPEND locally," Taleb wrote, according to CNBC-TV18.

"The US has long been benefiting from other countries' brain drain; without it its edge would collapse. Tesla, Von Braun, von Neumann, Fermi & Einstein did NOT each take the job of a citizen."

— Nassim Nicholas Taleb, author, The Black Swan

A brain-drain argument, pointed at India

Taleb went further than economics. "If the problem is anti-Indian racism, say it, don't play games," he wrote — a direct reference to the fact that Indian nationals receive the large majority of H-1B approvals each year and have borne the brunt of the current crackdown, from the $100,000 fee on new petitions to expanded social-media screening.

https://x.com/CNBCTV18Live/status/2111344275648831926

The comment arrives in the middle of the sharpest escalation yet. On October 8, the administration suspended the eight companies named above from the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) programme — the mandatory first step when an employer sponsors a foreign worker for an employment-based green card — citing ongoing federal investigations. Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said the department would "not accept or process any pending permanent labor certification applications involving these companies," and put the group's combined footprint at nearly three million foreign workers sought since 2009, with more than 230,000 H-1B approvals and over 100,000 labor certifications, India West reported.

The other side of the argument

Vice President JD Vance has framed the same facts in opposite terms. Announcing the Microsoft suspension, he said the company could not "lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants," pointing to roughly 6,000 US layoffs alongside thousands of H-1B approvals. Microsoft President Brad Smith has rejected the misuse allegation in a Politico interview and warned that restricting green-card access for skilled workers would weaken US technological competitiveness and push talent overseas — a dispute we covered in our report on Smith's pushback against Vance.

Taleb's intervention matters less for its novelty — economists have made the jobs-created argument for decades — than for its source and timing. He is neither an immigration advocate nor a tech executive, and his framing strips the debate to a single question: whether a job filled by a foreign worker is a job lost, or output gained. With PERM processing frozen for eight of the largest sponsors and investigations open, that question is now being answered by enforcement rather than argument.

What to watch

The administration has not released company-specific findings behind the PERM suspensions, and most of the named firms have not commented publicly. Until the investigations produce findings, employees at the eight companies sit in limbo: their H-1B status remains valid, but the green-card clock that PERM starts is stopped.
